models.summary: A cost-return model judges whether a global digital currency can live. The quantity of money is fixed, so rising demand means deflation, and the return is read as currency stability. The equation of exchange prices one unit, and purchasing power is set against a basket of goods, so the value depends only on the interest rate, income and the velocity of money. Faster cross-border settlement raises the efficiency of capital, which scales a Cobb-Douglas production function and lifts output. Capital availability is argued with supply and demand in the short run and the long run, and the central bank steers velocity so the rate settles near a benchmark. The three returns are then re-split into person, nation and world by fuzzy evaluation, with membership matrices and the maximum-membership rule. Cost splits into a hidden fundamental cost and a risk cost of three kinds, scored the same way. Net income is return minus cost, and the analytic hierarchy process weights each factor.

models.summary: Country choice is read through the Mundell-Fleming open-economy framework and the impossible trinity. Countries split by size. A large one sets the world rate and finances itself from home saving and foreign investment, so a rising rate cuts output fast enough that the rate cannot overshoot and settles. A small one only receives the world rate, and both a saving surplus flowing abroad and a saving shortfall used at home are called desirable. On the currency itself, the system already spends two of the trinity's three aims, free capital and no independent policy, so the exchange rate must be fixed. A country that keeps its own currency and floats it ends in rising prices. One that pegs holds output steady, and pegging is the only tool left once foreign-exchange reserves stop working.

models.summary: A three-level regulatory design replaces central-bank supervision once the technology itself, not state credit, earns trust. At the global level every account is a node, as in a blockchain, but one god node stands above the rest, owned by no country, shared by all and run by a body like the United Nations, coordinating cross-border investigations, and bound by a public international law so it is not abused. At the national level each authority keeps a lesser node, same powers but only at home, able to see through the whole domestic network to track laundering and freeze assets. At the personal level the shared ledger makes tax evasion easier to catch and lets a person read past transactions within limits. The claim is that no level is left unsupervised.

models.summary: Long-run effects are traced three ways. Banking profit grows at a constant rate before the digital currency spreads. After it, the growth rate falls linearly with acceptance and hits zero at a set acceptance level, so the on-balance-sheet business stops expanding and the bank becomes an investment intermediary. A simulation draws the curve. Regional effects are averages of the net income already computed, and since acceptance and velocity move together, acceptance is taken to its long-run ceiling and the net-income expressions are differentiated. The resulting matrix says the state gains the most at the margin, bears the least risk, and the person's gain is smallest and shrinking. Internationally, the paper sets the realist zero-sum view against a shared identity built on the technical frame and the law, and concludes that confrontation falls.
